content: Patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <22 mL/min) exhibit pharmacokinetics of tinidazole that are not significantly different from those observed in healthy individuals. However, during hemodialysis, the clearance of tinidazole is markedly increased, reducing its half-life from 12.0 hours to 4.9 hours. Approximately 43% of the tinidazole present in the body is eliminated during a 6-hour hemodialysis session. The pharmacokinetics of tinidazole in patients undergoing routine continuous peritoneal dialysis have not been studied. Additionally, there is no available data on the pharmacokinetics of tinidazole in patients with impaired hepatic function. Studies have reported reduced metabolic elimination of metronidazole, a chemically related nitroimidazole, in patients with hepatic dysfunction. Nonclinical toxicology studies have shown that metronidazole is carcinogenic in mice and rats but not in hamsters. Evidence of pulmonary, hepatic, and lymphatic tumorigenesis in mice, as well as mammary and hepatic tumors in female rats, has been observed in several studies. Carcinogenicity studies of tinidazole in rats, mice, or hamsters have not been reported. Tinidazole was found to be mutagenic in the TA100 strain of Salmonella typhimurium both with and without a metabolic activation system, but it was negative for mutagenicity in the TA98 strain. Mixed results (positive and negative) were observed in the TA1535, TA1537, and TA1538 strains. Tinidazole was also mutagenic in a tester strain of Klebsiella pneumoniae. However, it was negative for mutagenicity in a mammalian cell culture system using Chinese hamster lung V79 cells (HGPRT test system) and negative for genotoxicity in the Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) sister chromatid exchange assay. Tinidazole demonstrated positive in vivo genotoxicity in the mouse micronucleus assay. In a 60-day fertility study, tinidazole reduced fertility and caused testicular histopathology in male rats at a dose of 600 mg/kg/day, which is approximately three times the highest human therapeutic dose based on body surface area conversions. Spermatogenic effects were observed at doses of 300 and 600 mg/kg/day. The no-observed-adverse-reaction level (NOAEL) for testicular and spermatogenic effects was 100 mg/kg/day, approximately 0.5 times the highest human therapeutic dose based on body surface area conversions. These effects are characteristic of agents in the 5-nitroimidazole class. Acute toxicity studies in mice and rats revealed that the oral LD50 for mice was generally >3,600 mg/kg, and the intraperitoneal LD50 was >2,300 mg/kg. In rats, the LD50 was >2,000 mg/kg for both oral and intraperitoneal administration. A repeated-dose toxicology study in beagle dogs using oral tinidazole at doses of 100 mg/kg/day, 300 mg/kg/day, and 1,000 mg/kg/day for 28 days showed that the highest dose was reduced to 600 mg/kg/day on Day 18 due to severe clinical symptoms. Compound-related effects included increased thymus atrophy in both sexes at middle and high doses and prostate atrophy at all doses in males. A NOAEL of 100 mg/kg/day was determined for females, but no NOAEL was identified for males due to minimal prostate atrophy at 100 mg/kg/day, approximately 0.9 times the highest human dose based on plasma AUC comparisons. Clinical studies have extensively documented the use of tinidazole (2 g single oral dose) for trichomoniasis in over 2,800 patients across 34 published reports. In four blinded, randomized, comparative studies, cure rates assessed by culture ranged from 92% to 100%. In four additional studies assessed by wet mount, cure rates ranged from 80% to 100%. Tinidazole was found to be superior to placebo and comparable to other anti-trichomonal drugs. Open-label trials in men reported cure rates ranging from 83% to 100%. Tinidazole (2 g single dose) has also been documented for giardiasis in over 1,600 patients across 19 published reports. In eight controlled studies involving 619 subjects, cure rates ranged from 80% to 100%. Limited data compare a single 2 g dose of tinidazole to the usual 5-7 day regimen of metronidazole. For intestinal amebiasis, tinidazole has been documented in over 1,400 patients across 26 published reports, with most studies using 2 g/day for 3 days. Randomized controlled studies reported cure rates ranging from 86% to 93% after 3 days of therapy. Tinidazole use in amebic liver abscess has been documented in over 470 patients across 18 published reports, with most studies using 2 g/day for 2-5 days. Randomized controlled studies reported cure rates ranging from 81% to 100%, often accompanied by aspiration of the liver abscess when clinically necessary. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in 235 non-pregnant women evaluated the efficacy of tinidazole for bacterial vaginosis. Diagnosis was based on Amsel's criteria, requiring abnormal vaginal discharge with a pH >4.5, a fishy amine odor upon mixing with 10% KOH, and ≥20% clue cells on microscopic examination. Clinical cure required normalization of vaginal discharge and resolution of all Amsel's criteria. Microbiologic diagnosis was based on Gram stain demonstrating reduced or absent Lactobacillus morphology, predominance of Gardnerella morphotype, and few or absent white blood cells, with a Nugent score ≥4 required for inclusion and a score of 0-3 considered a microbiologic cure. Tinidazole demonstrated superior efficacy over placebo in achieving therapeutic, clinical, and microbiologic cures.
